- Louisiana v. Callais (2026): Louisiana's map with a second majority-Black district was an unconstitutional racial gerrymander; the Court said the Voting Rights Act did not require it.

Common questions:
Q: What does the 15th Amendment say in simple terms?
A: It says no government can deny or limit a citizen's right to vote because of race, color, or having once been enslaved. It applies to the federal government and every state. Congress can enforce it with laws such as the Voting Rights Act.
Q: When was the 15th Amendment ratified?
A: February 3, 1870. It was the last of the three Reconstruction Amendments passed after the Civil War. It followed the 13th, which ended slavery, and the 14th, which covers citizenship and equal protection.
Q: Did the 15th Amendment give women the right to vote?
A: No. It bans race discrimination in voting, but it says nothing about sex. Women won national protection for their vote in 1920, through the 19th Amendment.
Q: Why couldn't Black people vote after the 15th Amendment?
A: After Reconstruction, many states used poll taxes, literacy tests, grandfather clauses, threats, and violence to block Black voters. These tactics lasted for nearly 100 years. The Voting Rights Act of 1965 finally put the amendment into practice on a large scale.
Q: Is the Voting Rights Act still in effect?
A: Yes, but parts of it are narrower now. In Shelby County v. Holder (2013), the Court stopped the use of the formula for federal preapproval. In Louisiana v. Callais (2026), it read Section 2 more narrowly. Section 2 and other parts still apply.

## Sixteenth Amendment: Income tax
URL: https://freeconstitution.org/amendments/16/
Ratified: 1913-02-03

In one line: Congress can tax your income, from any source, without dividing the tax among the states by population.

Plain English: Congress has the power to tax incomes from any source, without apportioning the tax among the states based on population, and without regard to any census.

Myths vs. facts:
- Myth: The income tax is unconstitutional, or paying it is voluntary. Fact: Courts have rejected these claims many times. The Supreme Court upheld the income tax under this amendment in Brushaber v. Union Pacific Railroad (1916).
- Myth: The Sixteenth Amendment created the income tax. Fact: It gave Congress the power to tax income. Congress created the modern income tax by passing a law later in 1913.

Key cases:
- Pollock v. Farmers' Loan & Trust Co. (1895): A federal tax on income from property, such as rent and investments, had to be divided among the states by population.
- Brushaber v. Union Pacific Railroad Co. (1916): The federal income tax law of 1913 was constitutional under the Sixteenth Amendment.
- Moore v. United States (2024): Congress could tax American shareholders on a foreign company's income that the company earned but did not pay out to them.

Common questions:
Q: What does the 16th Amendment say in simple terms?
A: Congress can tax people's income, from any source. It does not have to divide the tax among the states by population. Ratified in 1913, it made a practical federal income tax possible.
Q: Is the income tax constitutional?
A: Yes. The 16th Amendment gives Congress the power to tax income. The Supreme Court upheld the federal income tax in Brushaber v. Union Pacific Railroad Co. (1916). Courts have rejected claims that the tax is unconstitutional or voluntary many times.
Q: Did the 16th Amendment create the income tax?
A: No. It gave Congress the power to tax income without dividing the tax among the states. Congress created the modern income tax by passing a law later in 1913.
Q: Why was the 16th Amendment passed?
A: To overcome a Supreme Court ruling. In Pollock v. Farmers' Loan & Trust Co. (1895), the Court said a tax on income from property had to be divided among the states by population. That made a practical income tax impossible.

## Seventeenth Amendment: Electing senators
URL: https://freeconstitution.org/amendments/17/
Ratified: 1913-04-08

In one line: Voters in each state elect their two U.S. senators directly. Before 1913, state lawmakers chose them.

Plain English: The U.S. Senate has two senators from each state, elected by the people of that state for six-year terms. Each senator has one vote. The voters who elect senators must meet the same qualifications required to vote for the larger house of their state legislature. When a Senate seat becomes vacant, the state's governor calls a special election to fill it. State legislatures may also authorize their governors to make temporary appointments until a special election can be held. This amendment does not affect senators who were already in office when it was ratified.

Myths vs. facts:
- Myth: Voters have always elected U.S. senators. Fact: For the first 124 years, state legislatures chose senators. Voters have elected them directly only since 1913.

Common questions:
Q: What does the 17th Amendment say in simple terms?
A: Voters in each state elect their two U.S. senators directly, for six-year terms. Before 1913, state legislatures chose senators. The amendment also explains how to fill a Senate seat that opens up.
Q: How were senators chosen before the 17th Amendment?
A: State legislatures chose them. The original Constitution set up this system in Article I. Some seats were won by bribing lawmakers, and others stayed empty when lawmakers could not agree.
Q: What happens when a senator dies or resigns?
A: The governor calls a special election to fill the seat. A state legislature can also let the governor appoint someone to serve until that election. The 17th Amendment allows both, and rules differ by state.
Q: When was the 17th Amendment ratified?
A: April 8, 1913. It came about two months after the 16th Amendment, during a period of reform. Many states had already held unofficial popular votes for senator before then.

## Eighteenth Amendment: Prohibition
URL: https://freeconstitution.org/amendments/18/
Ratified: 1919-01-16

In one line: This amendment banned making, selling, and transporting alcohol nationwide starting in 1920. It was repealed in 1933.

Plain English: Section 1. One year after this amendment is ratified, it becomes illegal to make, sell, transport, import, or export alcoholic beverages within the United States or any U.S. territory. Section 2. Congress and the states share the power to enforce this amendment by passing appropriate laws. Section 3. This amendment will not take effect unless ratified by three-fourths of the state legislatures within seven years. Note: This amendment was repealed by the Twenty-First Amendment in 1933. It is no longer in effect but remains in the Constitution as part of the document's record.

Myths vs. facts:
- Myth: Prohibition made drinking alcohol a crime. Fact: The amendment banned making, selling, and transporting alcohol for drinking. It did not ban drinking it.
- Myth: Since 1933, alcohol has been legal everywhere in the country. Fact: The Twenty-First Amendment let states keep their own bans. Some counties still ban alcohol sales today.

Key cases:
- National Prohibition Cases (1920): The Eighteenth Amendment was validly adopted, and the Volstead Act that enforced it was valid.

Common questions:
Q: What does the 18th Amendment say in simple terms?
A: It banned making, selling, and transporting alcoholic drinks in the United States, starting one year after ratification. This began Prohibition in January 1920. The 21st Amendment repealed it in 1933.
Q: Did Prohibition make drinking alcohol illegal?
A: No. The 18th Amendment banned making, selling, and transporting alcohol for drinking. It did not ban drinking it. The Volstead Act, the law that enforced Prohibition, set the limit at 0.5% alcohol.
Q: Why did Prohibition end?
A: Many people ignored the ban, and enforcement was hard and unpopular. A large illegal market grew, along with organized crime. During the Great Depression, many people also wanted the jobs and tax money from legal alcohol. The 21st Amendment ended it in 1933.
Q: Is the 18th Amendment still in effect?
A: No. The 21st Amendment repealed it on December 5, 1933. It is the only amendment ever fully repealed. Its text stays in the Constitution as part of the record.

## Nineteenth Amendment: Women's right to vote
URL: https://freeconstitution.org/amendments/19/
Ratified: 1920-08-18

In one line: No government can deny or limit your right to vote because of your sex.

Plain English: The right of U.S. citizens to vote cannot be denied or limited by the federal government or by any state because of sex. Congress has the power to enforce this amendment by passing appropriate laws.

Myths vs. facts:
- Myth: Women could not vote anywhere in the United States until 1920. Fact: Wyoming let women vote in 1869, while it was still a territory. By 1920, women already had full voting rights in more than a dozen states, mostly in the West.
- Myth: After 1920, every woman could vote. Fact: Many Black women in the South were blocked by poll taxes, reading tests, and threats until the Voting Rights Act of 1965. Many Native American women could not vote until Congress made Native Americans citizens in 1924, and some states blocked them longer.

Key cases:
- Minor v. Happersett (1875): Before this amendment, being a citizen did not by itself give women a constitutional right to vote.
- Leser v. Garnett (1922): The Nineteenth Amendment was validly adopted and applies in every state, including states that did not ratify it.

Common questions:
Q: What does the 19th Amendment say in simple terms?
A: No government can deny or limit a citizen's right to vote because of sex. It applies to the federal government and every state. Congress can pass laws to enforce it.
Q: When did women get the right to vote?
A: The 19th Amendment was ratified on August 18, 1920. It says the right to vote cannot be denied because of sex. Some states let women vote earlier, and many women of color still faced barriers after 1920.
Q: Could women vote before the 19th Amendment?
A: Yes, in some places. Wyoming let women vote in 1869, while it was still a territory. By 1920, women had full voting rights in more than a dozen states, mostly in the West. Before then, each state decided.
Q: Which state was the 36th to ratify the 19th Amendment?
A: Tennessee. It voted in August 1920, which met the three-fourths requirement. A 24-year-old lawmaker, Harry Burn, voted yes after his mother wrote asking him to.
Q: Could all women vote after 1920?
A: No. Many Black women in the South were blocked by poll taxes, reading tests, and threats until the Voting Rights Act of 1965. Many Native American women could not vote until Congress made Native Americans citizens in 1924, and some states blocked them longer.

## Twentieth Amendment: When terms begin
URL: https://freeconstitution.org/amendments/20/
Ratified: 1933-01-23

In one line: New Presidents start on January 20, and new members of Congress start on January 3, after the November election.

Plain English: Section 1. The terms of the President and Vice President end at noon on January 20. The terms of Senators and Representatives end at noon on January 3. New officials begin their terms at the same time. Section 2. Congress meets at least once a year, beginning at noon on January 3, unless Congress sets a different day by law. Section 3. If a President-elect dies before taking office, the Vice President-elect becomes President. If no President has been chosen by the start of the term, or if the President-elect has not qualified, the Vice President-elect serves as Acting President until a President qualifies. Congress can pass laws for what happens if neither has qualified. Section 4. Congress can pass laws for what happens if a candidate dies during certain stages of the presidential election process. Section 5. Sections 1 and 2 take effect on October 15 after ratification. Section 6. This amendment is void if not ratified within seven years.

Myths vs. facts:
- Myth: A President who loses the election leaves office right away. Fact: The outgoing President keeps full power until noon on January 20. This time between the election and the handover is often called the lame-duck period.

Common questions:
Q: What does the 20th Amendment say in simple terms?
A: New Presidents and Vice Presidents start their terms at noon on January 20. New members of Congress start at noon on January 3. It also says who takes over if a President-elect dies or is not ready.
Q: Why is Inauguration Day on January 20?
A: The 20th Amendment set that date. Before 1933, new Presidents took office on March 4, four months after the election. The amendment shortened that wait. The first January 20 inauguration was in 1937.
Q: What happens if the president-elect dies before Inauguration Day?
A: The Vice President-elect becomes President when the term begins. Section 3 of the 20th Amendment sets this rule. It has never been needed so far.
Q: Why is it called the Lame Duck Amendment?
A: A lame duck is an official still in office after someone else has been chosen to replace them. The 20th Amendment shortened that period. It moved the start of new terms closer to the November election.

## Twenty-first Amendment: Ending Prohibition
URL: https://freeconstitution.org/amendments/21/
Ratified: 1933-12-05

In one line: This amendment ended national Prohibition in 1933 and lets each state make its own alcohol laws.

Plain English: Section 1. The Eighteenth Amendment is repealed. Section 2. It is illegal to transport or import alcoholic beverages into any state, territory, or U.S. possession in violation of that place's laws. Section 3. This amendment will not take effect unless ratified by state conventions within seven years.

Myths vs. facts:
- Myth: The Twenty-First Amendment lets states do anything they want with alcohol. Fact: States still must follow the rest of the Constitution. In Granholm v. Heald (2005), the Court said states cannot treat out-of-state wineries worse than in-state ones.
- Myth: Prohibition was ended by a court. Fact: It was ended by this amendment, which states approved through special conventions.

Key cases:
- Craig v. Boren (1976): Oklahoma could not set a higher age for men than for women to buy low-alcohol beer, because that violated equal protection.
- Granholm v. Heald (2005): States cannot let in-state wineries ship directly to customers while blocking out-of-state wineries from doing the same.

Common questions:
Q: What does the 21st Amendment say in simple terms?
A: It ends national Prohibition by repealing the 18th Amendment. It also bans bringing alcohol into a state in a way that breaks that state's laws. That gives each state strong power over alcohol.
Q: Why did Prohibition end?
A: Many people ignored the ban, illegal alcohol was easy to find, and enforcement was unpopular. The Great Depression made many people want the jobs and tax money a legal industry could bring. The 21st Amendment repealed it on December 5, 1933.
Q: Does the 21st Amendment set the drinking age at 21?
A: No. The amendment does not mention a drinking age. Drinking ages come from state laws. States chose 21 after Congress tied highway money to that age, which the Court upheld in South Dakota v. Dole (1987).
Q: Why are alcohol laws different in every state?
A: Because Section 2 of the 21st Amendment gives states strong power over alcohol. Some counties still ban alcohol sales. States must still follow the rest of the Constitution, as Granholm v. Heald (2005) showed for out-of-state wineries.

## Twenty-second Amendment: Presidential term limits
URL: https://freeconstitution.org/amendments/22/
Ratified: 1951-02-27

In one line: No one can be elected President more than twice.

Plain English: Section 1. No person can be elected President more than twice. If a person has held the office of President, or served as Acting President, for more than two years of a term to which someone else was elected, that person can only be elected President once. This rule did not apply to the President in office when the amendment was proposed. Section 2. This amendment will not take effect unless ratified by three-fourths of state legislatures within seven years.

Myths vs. facts:
- Myth: A President can serve 8 years at most. Fact: A person could serve up to 10 years. They would first finish two years or less of another President's term, then win two elections.
- Myth: The two-term limit has always been in the Constitution. Fact: It was only a tradition until 1951. Franklin Roosevelt won four elections before the limit existed.

Common questions:
Q: What does the 22nd Amendment say in simple terms?
A: No one can be elected President more than twice. A person who serves more than two years of someone else's term can be elected only once. It was ratified in 1951.
Q: Can a president serve three terms?
A: No, not by election. The 22nd Amendment says no person shall be elected President more than twice. Franklin Roosevelt won four elections before the limit existed. He is the only President to serve more than two terms.
Q: What is the longest a president can serve?
A: About 10 years. A Vice President who takes over with two years or less left in someone else's term can still win two elections. Serving more than two years of that term allows only one election.
Q: Why was the 22nd Amendment passed?
A: Franklin Roosevelt won four elections, from 1932 to 1944. Before him, Presidents followed George Washington's two-term tradition, but no law required it. After Roosevelt died, Congress proposed the limit in 1947, and it was ratified in 1951.
Q: Could a two-term president become president another way?
A: This is debated, and no court has decided it. The 22nd Amendment bars being elected more than twice. Some argue a two-term President could still take over through succession. Others point to the 12th Amendment, which bars anyone constitutionally ineligible to be President from being Vice President.

## Twenty-third Amendment: D.C. votes for President
URL: https://freeconstitution.org/amendments/23/
Ratified: 1961-03-29

In one line: People who live in Washington, D.C., can vote for President. D.C. gets 3 electoral votes, the same as the smallest states.

Plain English: Section 1. Washington, D.C. — the seat of the federal government — appoints presidential electors. The number of D.C. electors equals what D.C. would have if it were a state, but never more than the least populous state has. These D.C. electors are in addition to those appointed by states and they participate in the presidential election under the same rules as state electors. Section 2. Congress has the power to enforce this amendment by passing appropriate laws.

Myths vs. facts:
- Myth: People in D.C. cannot vote in federal elections. Fact: Since 1964, they have voted for President. They also elect a House delegate who cannot vote to pass laws.
- Myth: D.C. has two senators, like a state. Fact: D.C. has no senators. This amendment covers only presidential elections.

Common questions:
Q: What does the 23rd Amendment say in simple terms?
A: People who live in Washington, D.C., can vote for President and Vice President. D.C. gets as many electoral votes as it would if it were a state, but never more than the smallest state. Today that is 3.
Q: How many electoral votes does Washington, D.C., have?
A: Three. The 23rd Amendment gives D.C. no more electoral votes than the least populous state, which has 3. D.C. voters first voted for President in 1964.
Q: Does D.C. have senators or a vote in Congress?
A: No. D.C. has no senators. It elects one delegate to the House, who can speak and work on committees but cannot vote to pass laws. The 23rd Amendment covers only presidential elections.
Q: Why couldn't D.C. vote for president before 1961?
A: The original Constitution gave electoral votes only to states. Washington, D.C., is not part of any state. The 23rd Amendment, ratified on March 29, 1961, gave D.C. electoral votes.

## Twenty-fourth Amendment: No poll taxes
URL: https://freeconstitution.org/amendments/24/
Ratified: 1964-01-23

In one line: No one can be charged a fee to vote in a federal election. A 1966 Supreme Court ruling extended this to state elections.

Plain English: Section 1. The right of U.S. citizens to vote in federal elections — for President, Vice President, presidential electors, U.S. Senators, or U.S. Representatives — cannot be denied or limited by the federal government or any state because of failure to pay a poll tax or other tax. Section 2. Congress has the power to enforce this amendment by passing appropriate laws.

Myths vs. facts:
- Myth: The Twenty-Fourth Amendment bans poll taxes in every election. Fact: The text covers only federal elections. Harper v. Virginia State Board of Elections (1966) banned poll taxes in state and local elections under the Fourteenth Amendment.
- Myth: Poll taxes were just small fees that did not stop anyone. Fact: For many poor families, the fee was a real cost, and in some states unpaid fees added up. That is why the tax kept many people from voting.

Key cases:
- Breedlove v. Suttles (1937): Georgia's poll tax did not violate the Constitution; this ruling was later overruled.
- Harman v. Forssenius (1965): Virginia could not make federal voters choose between paying a poll tax and filing a special residence certificate.
- Harper v. Virginia State Board of Elections (1966): Poll taxes in state elections violate the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.

Common questions:
Q: What does the 24th Amendment say in simple terms?
A: No one can be denied the vote in a federal election for failing to pay a poll tax or any other tax. Federal elections include those for President, Vice President, and Congress, and their primaries.
Q: What is a poll tax?
A: A poll tax is a fee a person must pay to be allowed to vote. After Reconstruction, many Southern states used poll taxes to keep Black citizens and poor citizens from voting. In 1964, five states still charged one.
Q: Are poll taxes illegal in state elections?
A: Yes. The 24th Amendment covers only federal elections. In Harper v. Virginia State Board of Elections (1966), the Court held that poll taxes in state elections violate the 14th Amendment. Together, they ended poll taxes in all U.S. elections.
Q: When was the 24th Amendment ratified?
A: January 23, 1964, during the civil rights movement. At that time, Alabama, Arkansas, Mississippi, Texas, and Virginia still charged poll taxes in federal elections. The amendment ended those taxes right away.
Q: Is voter ID a poll tax?
A: The Supreme Court has not ruled that it is. In Crawford v. Marion County Election Board (2008), the Court upheld Indiana's photo ID law for voting. It noted that Indiana offered free IDs. Critics say the papers needed to get an ID can cost money and burden voters. Supporters say free IDs mean no one pays to vote.

## Twenty-fifth Amendment: Presidential succession
URL: https://freeconstitution.org/amendments/25/
Ratified: 1967-02-10

In one line: If the President dies, resigns, or cannot do the job, the Vice President takes over, sometimes for only a few hours.

Plain English: Section 1. If the President is removed from office, dies, or resigns, the Vice President becomes President. Section 2. If the office of Vice President becomes vacant, the President nominates a Vice President. The new Vice President takes office once confirmed by a majority vote of both houses of Congress. Section 3. The President can voluntarily transfer power to the Vice President by sending a written declaration to the President pro tempore of the Senate and the Speaker of the House. The Vice President serves as Acting President until the President sends another written declaration ending the transfer. Section 4. The Vice President and a majority of either the Cabinet or another body designated by Congress can declare in writing that the President is unable to perform the duties of office. The Vice President then immediately serves as Acting President. If the President sends a written declaration that they are able to resume duties, the President resumes the office — unless the Vice President and the same majority send a second written declaration within four days that the President is still unable. In that case, Congress decides. Congress must convene within 48 hours if not in session. Congress has 21 days to reach a two-thirds vote in both houses that the President is unable. If both houses reach this vote, the Vice President continues as Acting President. Otherwise, the President resumes the office.

Myths vs. facts:
- Myth: The Twenty-Fifth Amendment is a quick way to remove a President people disagree with. Fact: Section 4 is about a President who is unable to do the job. If the President objects, it takes a two-thirds vote of both houses to keep the Vice President in charge. Section 4 has never been used.
- Myth: The Vice President has always clearly been able to fill in for a sick President. Fact: Before 1967, the Constitution did not say how to handle a President who was alive but unable to serve.

Common questions:
Q: What does the 25th Amendment say in simple terms?
A: If the President dies, resigns, or is removed, the Vice President becomes President. It also explains how to fill an empty vice presidency. And it sets rules for when a President cannot do the job, even for a short time.
Q: What happens if the president dies?
A: The Vice President becomes President. Section 1 of the 25th Amendment says this directly. The new President then nominates a new Vice President, who takes office once a majority of both houses of Congress approves.
Q: How does the 25th Amendment work?
A: It has four parts. Section 1 makes the Vice President President if the office opens. Section 2 fills an empty vice presidency. Section 3 lets a President hand over power for a time. Section 4 lets the Vice President and Cabinet act if the President cannot.
Q: Can the 25th Amendment remove a president?
A: Not exactly, and Section 4 has never been used. Under it, the Vice President and most of the Cabinet can declare the President unable to serve. The Vice President becomes Acting President. If the President objects, two-thirds of both houses must agree, or the President returns.
Q: Has the 25th Amendment ever been used?
A: Yes, several times. Gerald Ford became Vice President in 1973 and President in 1974 under it. George W. Bush and Joe Biden used Section 3 to hand over power briefly during medical procedures. Section 4 has never been used.
Q: What happens if the vice president dies or resigns?
A: The President nominates a new Vice President. That person takes office after a majority of both the House and the Senate votes to confirm. This happened with Gerald Ford in 1973 and Nelson Rockefeller in 1974.

## Twenty-sixth Amendment: Voting at 18
URL: https://freeconstitution.org/amendments/26/
Ratified: 1971-07-01

In one line: If you are a U.S. citizen and 18 or older, no government can stop you from voting because of your age.

Plain English: Section 1. The right of U.S. citizens age 18 or older to vote cannot be denied or limited by the federal government or any state because of age. Section 2. Congress has the power to enforce this amendment by passing appropriate laws.

Myths vs. facts:
- Myth: You have to be 21 to vote in some states. Fact: Since 1971, no state can set a voting age higher than 18 for any election.
- Myth: The amendment means no one under 18 can ever vote. Fact: It sets the highest age a government can require. A few cities, such as Takoma Park, Maryland, let 16- and 17-year-olds vote in city elections.
- Myth: College students cannot vote where they go to school. Fact: In most states, students can choose to register at their school address or their home address. Rules differ, so check with your state's election office.

Key cases:
- Oregon v. Mitchell (1970): Congress could set the voting age at 18 for federal elections but not for state and local elections.

Common questions:
Q: What does the 26th Amendment say in simple terms?
A: If you are a U.S. citizen and 18 or older, no government can deny or limit your right to vote because of your age. It covers federal, state, and local elections. Congress can pass laws to enforce it.
Q: Why is the voting age 18?
A: The 26th Amendment set it in 1971. During the Vietnam War, young men could be drafted at 18 but could not vote in most states until 21. Supporters used the slogan 'Old enough to fight, old enough to vote.'
Q: Can you vote at 17?
A: In some cases. Some states let 17-year-olds vote in a primary if they will be 18 by the general election. Many states let you register before you turn 18. Your state's election website or vote.gov has the rules.
Q: Can a city let 16-year-olds vote?
A: Yes. The 26th Amendment protects voters 18 and older. It does not ban a lower voting age. A few cities, such as Takoma Park, Maryland, let 16- and 17-year-olds vote in city elections.
Q: When was the voting age lowered to 18?
A: On July 1, 1971, when the 26th Amendment was ratified. It took about three months and one week after Congress passed it, the fastest ratification of any amendment. Before then, most states required voters to be 21.
Q: Can college students vote where they go to school?
A: Generally, yes. Students can usually choose to register at their school address or their home address. Rules differ by state, so check with your state's election office.

## Twenty-seventh Amendment: Congressional pay
URL: https://freeconstitution.org/amendments/27/
Ratified: 1992-05-07

In one line: If Congress votes to change its own pay, the change cannot start until after the next House election.

Plain English: No law that changes the pay of senators or representatives can take effect until after the next election for the House of Representatives.

Myths vs. facts:
- Myth: Congress cannot raise its own pay. Fact: It can. The raise just has to wait until after the next House election.

Common questions:
Q: What does the 27th Amendment say in simple terms?
A: If Congress changes its own pay, the change cannot take effect until after the next election for the House of Representatives. That gives voters a chance to respond before the change starts.
Q: Can Congress give itself a raise?
A: Yes. The 27th Amendment does not ban raises. It only says a pay change cannot start until after the next House election. Voters can decide whether to reelect members before the raise takes effect.
Q: Why did the 27th Amendment take 202 years to ratify?
A: James Madison proposed it in 1789, but not enough states ratified it then. Congress had set no deadline. In 1982, student Gregory Watson started a campaign to revive it. Enough states approved it by May 7, 1992.

## Article I: Congress
URL: https://freeconstitution.org/articles/1/

In one line: Congress makes federal laws. Article I sets up the House and Senate and lists what Congress and the states can and cannot do.

Sections:
- Section 1: Congress makes federal laws. It has two parts: the Senate and the House.
- Section 2: How the House works: two-year terms, who can serve, and how seats are divided.
- Section 3: How the Senate works: two senators per state, six-year terms, and impeachment trials.
- Section 4: States run congressional elections, but Congress can change the rules. Congress meets every year.
- Section 5: Each house sets its own rules, judges its members, and keeps a public record.
- Section 6: Members are paid, protected for speech in Congress, and cannot hold another federal office.
- Section 7: How a bill becomes a law, including the veto and how Congress can override it.
- Section 8: The list of Congress's powers, like taxing, trade, money, and declaring war.
- Section 9: Limits on Congress, like protecting habeas corpus and banning titles of nobility.
- Section 10: Limits on states, like no treaties, no coining money, and no war without Congress.

Common questions:
Q: What does Article I say in simple terms?
A: Article I creates Congress, the branch that makes federal laws. It sets up the House and the Senate. It lists Congress's powers, such as taxing and declaring war, and limits on what Congress and the states can do.
Q: What powers does Congress have?
A: Article I, Section 8 lists them. They include taxing, borrowing, regulating trade, coining money, declaring war, and raising armed forces. Congress can also pass laws necessary and proper to carry out these powers, as McCulloch v. Maryland (1819) confirmed.
Q: How does a bill become a law?
A: A bill must pass both the House and the Senate in the same form. Then it goes to the President, who can sign or veto it. Congress can override a veto with a two-thirds vote in each house. Article I, Section 7 sets these steps.
Q: How many senators does each state have?
A: Two. Article I, Section 3 gives every state two senators, no matter its size. Since the 17th Amendment (1913), voters in each state elect them directly for six-year terms.
Q: Why are there 435 members of the House?
A: A federal law sets that number, not the Constitution. Article I says House seats are divided among the states by population, counted every 10 years in the census. Congress fixed the size at 435 by law.
Q: What is the Commerce Clause?
A: It is the part of Article I that lets Congress regulate trade with other countries, among the states, and with Native American tribes. The Court read it broadly in Wickard v. Filburn (1942) and set limits in United States v. Lopez (1995).

## Article II: The President
URL: https://freeconstitution.org/articles/2/

In one line: The President carries out the laws, leads the military, makes treaties and appointments with the Senate, and can be removed by impeachment.

Sections:
- Section 1: The President's four-year term, how electors choose the President, who can serve, and the oath.
- Section 2: The President's powers: military command, pardons, treaties, and appointments with Senate approval.
- Section 3: The President's duties: report to Congress, receive ambassadors, and make sure laws are carried out.
- Section 4: The President and other officials can be impeached and removed for serious wrongdoing.

Common questions:
Q: What does Article II say in simple terms?
A: Article II creates the presidency. It says how the President is chosen and who can serve. It lists the President's powers, such as leading the military and making treaties and appointments with the Senate. It also allows removal by impeachment.
Q: How long is a president's term?
A: Four years. Article II sets a four-year term. The 22nd Amendment (1951) says no one can be elected President more than twice. The 20th Amendment says each term begins at noon on January 20.
Q: Who can be president?
A: Article II sets three rules. You must be a natural-born U.S. citizen, at least 35 years old, and a U.S. resident for at least 14 years. The 22nd Amendment adds that no one can be elected more than twice.
Q: Can a president be impeached?
A: Yes. The House can impeach a President for treason, bribery, or other high crimes and misdemeanors. The Senate then holds a trial, and two-thirds must vote to remove. Three Presidents have been impeached: Andrew Johnson, Bill Clinton, and Donald Trump (twice). None was removed.
Q: Can a president pardon anyone?
A: Only for federal crimes. Article II's pardon power does not cover state crimes. It cannot stop or undo an impeachment. A President can pardon someone before or after a conviction.
Q: Is the president immune from prosecution?
A: Partly. In Trump v. United States (2024), the Court held that a former President has absolute immunity for acts within his core constitutional powers. Other official acts get at least presumed immunity. Unofficial acts get no immunity.

## Article III: The courts
URL: https://freeconstitution.org/articles/3/

In one line: Article III creates the Supreme Court and other federal courts, gives judges life terms, guarantees jury trials for crimes, and defines treason narrowly.

Sections:
- Section 1: There is one Supreme Court, plus lower courts Congress creates. Judges serve for life.
- Section 2: Which cases federal courts can hear, and the right to a jury trial for crimes.
- Section 3: Treason means only making war on the country or helping its enemies, with strict proof.

Common questions:
Q: What does Article III say in simple terms?
A: Article III creates the Supreme Court and lets Congress create lower federal courts. Federal judges serve for life during good behavior. It lists which cases federal courts can hear, guarantees jury trials for federal crimes, and defines treason narrowly.
Q: How many Supreme Court justices are there?
A: The Constitution does not set a number. Congress sets it by law, and it is currently nine. It has been nine since 1869. Before then, Congress changed the number several times.
Q: What is judicial review?
A: It is the power of courts to strike down laws that conflict with the Constitution. Article III does not name this power. The Supreme Court claimed it in Marbury v. Madison (1803), and it has been accepted ever since.
Q: How long do Supreme Court justices serve?
A: For life, in practice. Article III says federal judges hold office during good behavior. They leave by retiring, resigning, dying, or impeachment and removal. Life terms are meant to protect judges from political pressure.
Q: What is treason in the Constitution?
A: Treason means only making war against the United States or helping its enemies. Article III requires two witnesses to the same act, or a confession in open court. Criticizing the government is not treason.

## Article IV: The states
URL: https://freeconstitution.org/articles/4/

In one line: States must respect each other's laws and court rulings, treat visitors fairly, and return people charged with crimes. Congress admits new states.

Sections:
- Section 1: States must accept each other's laws, records, and court rulings.
- Section 2: States must treat visitors fairly and return people charged with crimes. Includes the Fugitive Slave Clause.
- Section 3: Congress admits new states and makes rules for federal land and territories.
- Section 4: The nation promises each state an elected government and protection from invasion.

Common questions:
Q: What does Article IV say in simple terms?
A: Article IV covers how states treat each other. States must respect each other's records and court rulings, treat visitors fairly, and return people charged with crimes. Congress admits new states, and every state is promised an elected government.
Q: What is the Full Faith and Credit Clause?
A: It requires each state to generally accept the laws, records, and court rulings of other states. For example, a final court judgment from one state can generally be enforced in another. It is in Article IV, Section 1.
Q: What is extradition in the Constitution?
A: Extradition means sending a person charged with a crime back to the state where it happened. Article IV, Section 2 requires it. In Puerto Rico v. Branstad (1987), the Court said federal courts can order a governor to do this.
Q: How does a new state join the United States?
A: Congress admits it. Article IV, Section 3 gives Congress this power. A new state cannot be made from part of an existing state without the consent of that state's legislature and Congress.

## Article V: Changing the Constitution
URL: https://freeconstitution.org/articles/5/

In one line: An amendment needs two-thirds of Congress, or a convention called by two-thirds of states, to propose it, then three-fourths of states to ratify.


Common questions:
Q: What does Article V say in simple terms?
A: Article V explains how to change the Constitution. Two-thirds of both houses of Congress, or a convention called by two-thirds of the states, can propose an amendment. Three-fourths of the states must then ratify it.
Q: How is the Constitution amended?
A: In two steps. First, two-thirds of the House and Senate propose an amendment, or a convention called by two-thirds of the states does. Then three-fourths of the states, 38 of 50, must ratify it. Every amendment so far was proposed by Congress.
Q: Does the president sign constitutional amendments?
A: No. The President has no formal role in amending the Constitution. In Hollingsworth v. Virginia (1798), the Court said a proposed amendment does not need the President's signature.
Q: How many amendments have been proposed?
A: More than 11,000 amendments have been proposed in Congress since 1789. Only 27 have been ratified. The first 10, known as the Bill of Rights, were ratified together in 1791.

## Article VI: The supreme law
URL: https://freeconstitution.org/articles/6/

In one line: The Constitution, federal laws, and treaties are the supreme law. Officials must swear to support the Constitution, and no religious test is allowed.


Common questions:
Q: What does Article VI say in simple terms?
A: Article VI makes the Constitution, federal laws, and treaties the supreme law of the land. It keeps debts from before the Constitution. It requires officials to swear or affirm support for the Constitution and bans religious tests for federal office.
Q: What is the supremacy clause?
A: It is the part of Article VI that makes the Constitution, valid federal laws, and treaties the supreme law of the land. When a valid federal law conflicts with a state law, the federal law wins. State judges must follow it.
Q: Can a state ignore federal law?
A: No. States cannot nullify valid federal law. In Cooper v. Aaron (1958), the Court said state officials are bound by its rulings on the Constitution. But in Printz v. United States (1997), it said Congress cannot order state officers to carry out federal programs.
Q: What is the No Religious Test Clause?
A: It says no one can be required to pass a religious test to hold federal office. A religious test is a rule that you must belong to, or swear to, a certain faith. Officials may also affirm instead of swear.

## Article VII: Approving the Constitution
URL: https://freeconstitution.org/articles/7/

In one line: The Constitution would take effect once conventions in nine of the thirteen states ratified it.


Common questions:
Q: What does Article VII say in simple terms?
A: Article VII says the Constitution would take effect once conventions in nine states ratified it, and only among those states. It also records that the Convention finished the Constitution on September 17, 1787.
Q: When was the Constitution ratified?
A: New Hampshire became the ninth state to ratify on June 21, 1788, which was enough for the Constitution to take effect. The last of the 13 states, Rhode Island, ratified in May 1790.
Q: How many states had to ratify the Constitution?
A: Nine of the 13. Article VII set that number so one or two holdouts could not block the new system. Each state voted through a special convention.
Q: Why is Constitution Day on September 17?
A: It is the day the delegates signed the Constitution in 1787. Article VII records that date. George Washington signed as President of the Convention, along with 38 other delegates from twelve states.

## The Preamble
URL: https://freeconstitution.org/preamble/

In one line: The Preamble says the people are making the Constitution and lists six goals. It does not give anyone powers or rights by itself.

Common questions:
Q: What does the Preamble say in simple terms?
A: It says the people of the United States are making the Constitution, and it lists why. The goals are a better union, justice, peace at home, defense, the general welfare, and liberty for now and the future.
Q: What are the six goals of the Preamble?
A: The six goals are a more perfect union, justice, domestic tranquility, the common defense, the general welfare, and the blessings of liberty. In plain words: unity, fairness, peace, defense, well-being, and freedom.
Q: Does the Preamble give you any rights?
A: No. The Preamble states the Constitution's goals. In Jacobson v. Massachusetts (1905), the Court said it is not a source of government power. Your rights come from other parts of the Constitution.
Q: What does "We the People" mean?
A: It means the Constitution's authority comes from the people, not from a king or the state governments. An earlier draft listed the states by name instead. In 1787, though, many people, including most women and enslaved people, could not vote.

## The Declaration of Independence
URL: https://freeconstitution.org/declaration/

In one line: The Declaration announced in 1776 that the colonies were independent from Britain. It explains why, but it is not law.

Common questions:
Q: What does the Declaration of Independence say in simple terms?
A: It says the 13 colonies are free and independent states, no longer ruled by Britain. It says "all men are created equal," with rights to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. It then lists the King's abuses as reasons.
Q: Is the Declaration of Independence law?
A: No. It is not law and not part of the Constitution. Courts do not enforce it, and you cannot sue under it. Your legal rights come from the Constitution and other laws.
Q: Who wrote the Declaration of Independence?
A: Thomas Jefferson wrote the first draft. Benjamin Franklin, John Adams, and others made edits. The Second Continental Congress approved it on July 4, 1776, in Philadelphia.
Q: What is the difference between the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution?
A: The Declaration announced independence in 1776 and explained why. The Constitution, written in 1787 and ratified in 1788, set up the government and is the supreme law. Only the Constitution is law that courts enforce.
